title: SEJDOVIC et SULEJMANOVIC contre l'ITALIE
conclusion: Partiellement recevable;Partiellement irrecevable (Art. 35) Conditions de recevabilité;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae
summary: In the case of Sejdovic and Sulejmanovic v. Italy, the applicants, Fatima Sejdovic and Izet Sulejmanovic, are Roma from the former Yugoslavia, who brought the case on their own behalf and that of their minor children against Italy. Their Roma identity placed them in a particularly vulnerable position, as they faced both the precariousness of life as migrants and the specific marginalisation experienced by Roma and Travellers in Europe. After fleeing Bosnia-Herzegovina, the family settled in the Casilino 700 camp in Rome, a spontaneous settlement known for its dire living conditions and lack of basic sanitation. In 1999 and 2000, following a census and increased police surveillance, the Italian authorities issued expulsion orders against the applicants, citing irregular immigration status, and ultimately removed them from Italy in March 2000. The applicants argued that their expulsion exposed them and their children to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that they lacked effective remedies, raising issues under Article 13. The Court found the case partially admissible, deciding that the applicants’ complaints about expulsion and the risk of ill-treatment warranted further examination on the merits. This case highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe, particularly regarding forced evictions and the lack of adequate procedural safeguards, against a backdrop of historical exclusion and discrimination.
